newsitem.title: USA: US rate volatility unnerves emerging market bonds.
newsitem.headline: US rate volatility unnerves emerging market bonds.

text.p: The gyration of U.S. Treasuries and a sliding U.S. dollar sent a chill through the emerging markets, forcing a surrender of early gains by Friday's close, traders and analysts said.
Thanks to the recovered strength of the Treasuries, the emerging debts managend to retain a fraction of the gains, while underperforming the Treasuries.

An early spell of euphoria was credited to comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan that were interpreted as hinting the Fed might not raise rates in the May 20 meeting. But that was followed by a selloff, then a rebound.
Sentiments in the emerging market followed the roller coaster ride of the Treasuries, the market sources said.

"We still see a probability of tightening in May," said Luis R. Luis, head of emerging market analysis at Scudder Stevens and Clark. "The U.S. yield curve market has priced in (a rate hike), but the emerging markets have not fully discounted the rise."
In a Reuters survey of economists in the United States and Canada, 19 out of 26 forecast a 25-basis -point rise in the federal funds rate at the May 20 meeting of Fed policy makers.
The recent rally in emerging markets reflected the still-ample global liquidity despite many disquieting signs, said Kip Allardt, strategist at CS First Boston.

Investors who had adopted defensive positions were putting the money to work, even though the current interest rate environment is fraught with risk to leveraged bond positions, he said. "The far end of the credit curve will have more volatility and will be adversely impacted."
The emerging market bonds, by implication, would face some hard knocks, Allardt said.
Gary Evans, global debt strategist at UBS Securities, said the volatility of the Treasuries made the trading of emerging market assets very choppy.
"Traders on the street are getting whipsawed," he said. "It's not a happy camp out there."
The credit tightening in Japan and the onset of the U.S. dollar's slide portended more uncertainty ahead, he said.
The dollar hit three-month low at 119 yen before trimming losses. A weak dollar diminish the luster of investing in emerging market bonds, of which many are dollar-based.

Traders said high-yielders like Bulgaria and Ecuador bonds led the early rally, in which par bonds also did better than discounts. When the sentiment turned mixed, high-yielders shed the gains and traded in tandem with the rest of the market, they said.
In late afternoon, Argentina FRBs ARFLC05=RR and Brazil C BR8D14=RR were each up 1/4 at 92-1/4 and 76-3/4 bid.

Venesuela debts managed to hold on to most of the gains. DCB bonds VZFLL07=RR rose 5/8 to 89-1/8 bid. The country's large current account surplus was cited as a good cushion against external interest rate shocks.
Polish and Russian debts also escaped much of the selling. Poland PDI PO325024=RR gained 5/8 to 83-5/8 bid and Russian dollar Vnesh RUVNUSLNS=RR added 1/8 to 83-1/4 bid.
